tagline.text: A legendary mountain standing alone above the endless Pampanga plain

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,000–2,500 per person (day trip from Manila, including shared guide fee)

children.text: An old volcano about 1,026m high, standing alone amid the endless rice fields of central Luzon. Follow forest trails steeped in the legend of mountain spirit Sinukuan to the summit, where the Pampanga plain and, in the distance, Mount Pinatubo unfold below — a peak climbable in a day trip from Manila.
Mount Arayat is a stratovolcano about

high, straddling Arayat and Magalang in Pampanga province. Surrounded entirely by flat rice paddies and sugarcane fields, it's a landmark of central Luzon visible from almost anywhere along NLEX or SCTEX. A collapsed crater opens to the northwest, with the highest peak, the North Peak, and a ring of summits along the southeastern rim, and the whole mountain is covered in dense forest.

Geologically, it's an old volcano that was active hundreds of thousands of years ago, with no eruptions recorded in historical times, though it's still classified as potentially active. Its slopes were designated a national park in
and redesignated a protected landscape under the national protected-area system in
. During World War II, it also served as a base for the anti-Japanese guerrilla group the Hukbalahap.

To the Kapampangan people, Arayat is a sacred mountain, home to the mountain spirit Sinukuan (Mariang Sinukuan). As the story goes, Sinukuan once shared fruit and meat with villagers, but when greedy people started stealing it, she turned the fruit to stone and vanished from sight. The White Rock near the southern peak is believed to be where she lives, and legend also tells of her battling the spirit of Mount Pinatubo.

There are broadly two trails: one climbing from the Magalang side to the highest North Peak, and another climbing from the national park on the Arayat side to the South Peak, with a traverse connecting the two forming a long route for experienced hikers. Though not especially high above sea level, the mountain rises straight up from flat land, making the climb steep, with rope sections along the way, so beginners should start with the North Peak round trip. Even without hiking, it's worth stopping by for the national park's picnic grounds at the base and Arayat's famous halo-halo.

blocks.title: Climbing to the North Peak summit

children.text: Starting from Ayala village in Magalang, the trail crosses rice paddies and forest to the highest North Peak, taking about
3–5 hours
one way. The final stretch is steep, so save some energy. On a clear day, you can see all the way past the plain to Mount Pinatubo and the Zambales Mountains.

blocks.title: The South Peak and White Rock

children.text: This route climbs from the national park side in San Juan Bano, Arayat, with a thrilling rope-assisted rock-climbing section. From the open, viewpoint-like rocks, the Pampanga River and rice fields spread out below like a mosaic.
A long route, about
10–12 hours
, climbing up one side and descending the other. Recommended for hikers with prior experience and good fitness — you'll need to start before sunrise to make it down before dark.

The national park at the southern foot of the mountain has shaded trees, a pool, and picnic huts, making it a good half-day spot for family travelers who aren't hiking. It gets crowded with local families on weekends.

blocks.title: Sunrise and sunset over the plain

children.text: Starting the North Peak climb before dawn lets you watch the sun rise over the plain along the way up. The mountain's silhouette at sunset, seen from the Pampanga riverbank or the rice paddies below, is beautiful too.
A halo-halo shop that has been running in Arayat since the
, known nationwide for its simple recipe of just three toppings — mashed kidney beans, carabao-milk pastillas, and cream corn. A bowl after the descent is the best reward.
Ask your guide to tell you the story of the mountain spirit Sinukuan. Walking while hearing the tales tied to the huge boulders and old trees along the trail makes the climb all the more interesting.

In the wet season,
June–October

, the red-dirt trail turns to mud and gets very slippery, making the rope sections dangerous. Trails are sometimes closed after typhoons or heavy rain, so it's best to avoid this period. In any season, midday temperatures run high, so the basic plan is to start before sunrise, tag the summit in the morning, and descend.

Most visitors come for the day, but for a dawn climb by public transport, it's more convenient to stay the night before in Angeles/Clark or San Fernando. Clark has plenty of hotels and resorts around
per night, and business hotels in downtown Angeles or San Fernando run about
. Magalang and Arayat also have small resorts and homestays, but facilities are basic, so check reviews in advance. Camping on the mountain is allowed only with a permit.

A stop you shouldn't skip after the descent is Kabigting's halo-halo in Arayat. Instead of dozens of toppings, it uses only mashed kidney beans, carabao-milk pastillas, and cream corn, for a soft, sweet flavor. For meals, it's worth trying original sisig in Angeles or classic Kapampangan cooking in San Fernando, both about
30–40 minutes
away by car. Small shops near the trailhead sell drinks and simple meals, but they may not be open in the early pre-dawn hours.
A guide and registration are required. Guides can be in short supply on weekends, so book ahead through the trailhead office or a local guide's contact.
There's almost no reliable water source along the trail. Bring at least 2–3 liters of water per person, more for the traverse.
With rope sections and steep dirt slopes, bring hiking shoes with good grip, gloves, and trekking poles.
Start before sunrise to avoid the midday heat. A headlamp is essential.
If it's your first time, try the North Peak round trip first, and save the traverse for after you've built up experience on other mountains.
The forest can have mosquitoes and leeches. Bring insect repellent and long socks.
Carry all your trash out, and respect local beliefs about the mountain spirit by avoiding loud noise or damage to the surroundings.

Registration and a guide are required by rule on Mount Arayat, and trails can close without notice during high wildfire risk, heavy wet-season rain, or for maintenance. Check the latest notices from the Arayat/Magalang local government and the protected-area management office before you set out.
The red-dirt trail and rocks get very slippery when it rains. Avoid hiking in the wet season and crossing the rope sections in the rain.
The long, steep climb carries a risk of dehydration and heatstroke. Take plenty of rest breaks and replenish fluids and salt.
There are many unmarked side trails, making it easy to get lost. Stay with your guide and descend before sunset.
If you leave a car at the national park or trailhead, don't leave valuables visible inside.
Camping and open fires are allowed only in designated spots. Even a small spark can spread into a wildfire during the dry season.
